newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legal challenge to interim assembly seen futile.
newsitem.headline: HK legal challenge to interim assembly seen futile.

text.p: A court challenge by the popular Democratic Party against a China-appointed shadow legislature was branded a futile exercise by Hong Kong legal experts on Friday.

Hong Kong's Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that the Democrats could use government funds to challenge laws passed by the provisional assembly, set to replace the currently elected body after China takes over from the British on July 1.
The Democrats, who hold 19 seats and have much to lose when the Legislative Council is disbanded in just 25 days, said it was constitutionally illegal to have two legislatures at the same time.
A Democratic Party spokesman said it would challenge the interim body in the next few days for embarking on legislative activities before July 1 when the territory becomes a Special region of China.

In transition from British to Beijing's rule, Hong Kong has twin legislatures, a non-elected assembly-in-waiting that meets across the border in the South China city of Shenzhen and the doomed, elected assembly in Hong Kong.
"Even if they win (the suit), it will not have much effect on the operation of the provisional legislature after July 1," Albert Chan, dean of Hong Kong University Law Faculty, told Reuters.
Another law expert, Nihal Jayawickrama, also of Hong Kong University, said it was an ill-judged move to sue the interim body before the July 1 changeover.
"I think it is unwise to challenge now because what it has done so far has not in any way affected anybody in Hong Kong," he told Reuters.
"There has to be an impact...someone must be affected by the laws passed by the provisional legislature, so I think the challenge must come after July," he said.
The English-language South China Morning Post also said the challenge came a little too late.
"This battle has begun very late in the day, and the possibility must be fully resolved before the provisional legislature, itself, has gone out of existence," it said.
A pro-China academic Lau Siu-kai said the Democrats' move was to "embarrass China and the Special Administrative Region government".

Pro-Beijing newspapers also swung into action on Friday criticising the law suit as a "farce" orchestrated by Britain, which has run Hong Kong for 156 years after seizing it from Imperial China's Manchu Dynasty.

"Meddling by a British-Hong Kong court in the work of the provisional legislature will not undermine the progress of China resuming Hong Kong's sovereignty," the China-funded Wen Wei Po daily said. "But the interference by the British-Hong Kong court is clearly a move to create troubles during the soverignty transfer on July 1."
